C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK.Name: Updater rollback: one-step restore of the previous version from the Help menu or a terminal command when the UI will not start
C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK.Summary: The desktop updater today can only move forward: installSignedUpdate (src/renderer/src/commands/index.js:1195-1217) calls downloadAndInstall and relaunches, the old bundle is replaced in place, and nothing anywhere keeps a copy (verified: no backup or preserve code near the updater; the updater feed is a single forward-only latest.json on GitHub Releases). If a shipped release breaks startup, the only recovery is a manual download from the release-history page. This change ships a one-step rollback modeled on the JetBrains Toolbox rule ("keeps a previously installed version … to enable instant rollback"): before every in-app update Mark snapshots the running version — on macOS a copy of the current .app bundle plus the canonical preferences file under the M-022 data root in rollback/, with SHA-256 digests recorded in a rollback manifest; on Windows the manifest records only the previous version, and the restore fetches that version's installer from GitHub Releases and verifies it with the same minisignature scheme the updater itself uses (the signature published in that release's latest.json asset, checked against the updater pubkey pinned in the app). Restore is reachable two ways: a Help-menu item "Roll Back to Mark {version}…" with a confirmation that names the settings-revert caveat, and a --rollback CLI flag parsed in M-020 before the UI boots, so a user whose window never opens can restore from Terminal — documented with the exact commands per OS in the mark-site guides (guide/faq.md and guide/cli.md). Every restore re-verifies the staged state before touching anything, restores the pre-update preferences snapshot, and sets the existing skippedUpdateVersion key to the departed version, so the updater does not immediately re-offer the version the user just escaped. Exactly one rollback set is kept and refreshed by each successful update; app-store builds (MAS, TestFlight) get no rollback surface at all.

Problem.Description: (1) One bad release can strand every auto-updated desktop user. The update flow lives entirely inside the UI: the launch-time check (src/renderer/src/store/autoUpdates.js), the notice card with the Update button (src/renderer/src/components/updateNotice/index.vue:83-88), and the Settings row all assume a working window. If the new version crashes at boot, none of those surfaces exist, and the user's only recourse is to know that mark.xronocode.com keeps a release-history page and to reinstall an old DMG or EXE by hand. (2) The blast radius is not hypothetical: the 2.8.0 release train already lived the scenario — a field regression (FIX-017) that did not hold through three aborts before FIX-018 landed (docs/release-trains/2.7.x-next.md, the 2.8.0 FIX-017/FIX-018 entry) — and recovery for affected users meant waiting for the next release, because the updater serves a single latest.json to the whole desktop fleet within 24 hours (launch-time check, once per day, default on). (3) The escape-hatch pattern is standard where updates can break work: JetBrains Toolbox keeps the previous installed version "to enable instant rollback", Windows offers "Go back" for 10 days after an upgrade, TestFlight lists previous builds, and Chrome's enterprise rollback documents the exact price (user data written by the newer version may not survive) — a price Mark must also pay deliberately via a preferences snapshot. (4) Mark already ships half the mechanism: "Skip this version" (skippedUpdateVersion, autoUpdates.js:58) prevents an unwanted re-offer, but nothing exists to go back once an update is installed. (5) Preferences are only protected against torn writes (atomic rename, m005_prefs.rs), not against a rollback reading a file the old code does not understand — the schema_version stamp never errors (m005_prefs.rs:173-184), so a snapshot-and-restore step is needed to make the old version boot with known-good settings.

Goals.R-1: Snapshot-before-update (fail-closed): the update path gains a preparation step (a new Rust command, e.g. mt_rollback::prepare) invoked from installSignedUpdate before downloadAndInstall. On macOS it stages a copy of the currently running .app bundle plus the canonical M-005 preferences file into rollback/ under the M-022 data root; the manifest records the previous version, platform, staged paths, SHA-256 digests of both staged artifacts and a timestamp. On Windows it writes the same manifest with only the validated previous version (the asset name and URL are derived from that version at restore time, never stored). If the snapshot cannot be created and digested, the update aborts with a clear message and the current version keeps running — an update is never applied without a restorable state. The fresh snapshot is promoted to the live set (replacing any older set) only after the update has been applied successfully, immediately before relaunch or exit: a failed download or install leaves the previous live set untouched, so an escape hatch is never destroyed by a failed attempt to escape. Staging is atomic (temp sibling, then rename) so an interrupted snapshot never presents itself as valid, and a stale temp sibling left by an interrupted run is removed at the next prepare or restore.
Goals.R-2: Windows restore source and verification: the restore on Windows downloads the previous version's installer (Mark_{version}_x64-setup.exe from the v{version} GitHub release, the exact naming produced by release.yml) and verifies it with the updater's own trust anchor: the signature published for that platform in the release's latest.json asset, checked with the minisign scheme against the updater pubkey pinned in the app — the same verification the updater performs on every update; integrity and authenticity are both covered by that pinned-anchor check (the Windows installer is not OS-code-signed today). The fetched feed's version field must equal the manifest's previous version before its platform entry is used. Only the deterministically derived release asset may ever be fetched or executed; the manifest carries the previous version under strict semver and any manifest whose stored data disagrees with the derivation is rejected before any network access (pinned by a test that injected path or URL material fails closed with nothing fetched). Coverage preconditions, recorded honestly: Windows release assets exist only for releases published with the WINDOWS_RELEASE repo variable enabled (release.yml stages the Windows artifact set behind it), so Windows rollback spans exactly those releases; and restore verification uses the updater pubkey pinned in the currently running app, so releases signed before any future key rotation would fail verification (exit 4) — in both cases the message points to the release-history page for a manual download, the plan confirms the variable for the versions in scope, and the FAQ documents the fallback.
Goals.R-3: Restore execution (verify first, fail closed): before any swap, the manifest is validated (strict schema, semver-strict version, platform match, staged paths contained under the data root) and the staged artifacts are re-verified against the recorded SHA-256 digests; an invalid manifest behaves exactly like a missing one (no menu item, CLI exit 7, nothing applied) — validity also rejects, defensively, a manifest whose recorded previous version equals the currently running version (the failed-attempt state: R-1's promote-only-after-success prevents it from arising, validity guarantees it can never surface even if it does); a digest mismatch aborts with the current state untouched (exit 6). On macOS the staged previous .app is swapped over the current bundle path (the path the app actually runs from — never a hardcoded /Applications), moving the departed bundle to Trash so it can be inspected; an unwritable bundle path fails closed (exit 6, clear message, no privileged helpers, never a half-swap), a Trash failure after a successful swap is logged and non-blocking; after the swap the preferences snapshot is restored over the canonical preferences file and skippedUpdateVersion is written to the departed version (the existing key and semantics from autoUpdates.js, exact-version match) — the bundle swap strictly precedes both writes. The staged-copy digests are self-consistent (they live in the same user-writable manifest as the copy); this is the consciously accepted bound — the swap runs as the user, and a same-user attacker already has easier paths — and the same accepted same-user bound applies to the Windows staging directory and its version-only manifest (the pinned-key minisign anchor covers the network fetch, not local tampering by the same user). On Windows the ordering inverts by necessity, because the running process cannot observe its own replacement: the preferences snapshot is restored and skippedUpdateVersion written while the process still runs — as the last writes before the spawn, after pending preference writes from the live renderer have quiesced (exact sequencing fixed at plan time) — then the verified installer is spawned in passive mode and the process exits immediately with success (its outcome is pending and the output says so) — the executed installer is the verified installer (its bytes are re-digested, or it is spawned from the verified handle, immediately before execution). The rollback manifest is finalized only after the install is confirmed successful, by the restored version detecting at its next launch that it is running the manifest's previous version and deleting the staging directory; if the installer run failed, the still-departed version detects at its next launch that it is not running the manifest's previous version, keeps the set, and the rollback surface stays available for an idempotent retry. On both platforms a successful restore deletes the entire staging directory — manifest, staged artifacts and preferences snapshot, on Windows at next-launch finalization — so a rollback cannot chain into another rollback; concurrent restore invocations during the Windows pending window are serialized by a staging-area lock or marker (exact mechanism fixed at plan time, so a second headless run cannot re-spawn the installer); the app relaunches (on Windows the installer's completion hands over to the relaunched app). Every step emits structured log markers (e.g. [Rollback][prepare|verify|restore][BLOCK_*]) suitable for verification entries.
Goals.R-4: In-app surface: a desktop-only Help-menu item "Roll Back to Mark {version}…" (m009_menu.rs, command id in the existing taxonomy) that is present only when a valid rollback manifest exists. Activating it opens a confirmation dialog that names exactly what happens: the app returns to {version}, settings return to their pre-update snapshot (changes made after updating are reverted), and {departed version} will not be re-offered until a newer release ships. Cancel changes nothing. The rollback command exposed to the renderer re-validates the full restore preconditions in Rust before acting; the dialog is its only intended entry, and the renderer exposure is knowingly accepted (the same capability class as the already renderer-exposed downloadAndInstall).
Goals.R-5: CLI crash-recovery: a --rollback flag in the M-020 clap parser, handled in main.rs before the window is created, runs the same restore headless: it prints each step to the terminal and asks y/N when stdin is a TTY, printing the same three facts the dialog names — the target version, the settings revert to the pre-update snapshot, and the skip of the departed version; only the exact wording is deferred to the plan. The app-store gate (exit 3) is evaluated first, then manifest validity is resolved locally: an invalid set reports exit 7 regardless of whether an instance is live, and a store build never reads a stray desktop-era manifest. Because the single-instance plugin is registered only later during app init, the pre-boot handler itself probes for a live instance (concrete mechanism fixed at plan time): if one answers, it delegates by asking the running instance to open the in-app confirmation dialog (R-4) and exits without performing restore work — no headless swap under a running app, no second process; a successful delegation is also exit 0, distinguished from a restore by its machine-readable output line; an instance that acknowledges the probe but cannot show the dialog (a broken renderer) must not strand the CLI path either way — after a short acknowledgment timeout the command declines without performing any restore work, exits 6, and prints that Mark must be quit before rerunning for the headless restore (the FAQ carries the same advice; no swap is ever performed under a live instance). Non-interactive runs require an explicit --yes; without a TTY and without --yes the command declines (a scripted restore must be deliberate). Exit codes are deterministic and documented in the guide: 0 restored and relaunched, successfully delegated to the running instance, or (Windows) the verified installer spawned with its outcome pending; 3 app-store build (prints the same "Updates are managed by the App Store" voice as mt_updater_check); 4 Windows download or minisign verification failure; 5 declined at the prompt or missing --yes non-interactively; 6 restore failed or not performed — including a live instance that cannot show the dialog — with details in output; 7 no valid rollback set (prints where to find release-history). Code 2 is left to clap's own usage-error exit and is never reassigned; the guide's exit table says so.
Goals.R-6: One-step depth, bounded footprint: exactly one rollback set exists. Each successful update replaces the set with the newer snapshot and cleans the previous staged copy; a successful restore deletes the entire staging directory (manifest, staged artifacts and preferences snapshot). No version vault, no side-by-side installs, no rollback history. The staged copy lives under the M-022 data root (Application Support on macOS), not inside the shipped bundle, so the on-disk budget of the app itself is not affected by staging (staged copies live in the data root); this change's additions — the new module and locale strings — must not grow the shipped macOS bundle beyond the recorded baseline (≈ 32 MB on disk at v2.8.2; the historical under-30 MB Phase-B on-disk target is a pre-existing miss this change does not worsen), and the CI-enforced 20 MB Windows installer gate keeps passing; the steady-state data-root cost is one bundle copy on macOS and one small manifest on Windows, with a transient 2x-bundle peak in the data root during staging and refresh (the temp sibling beside the live set), which the data root absorbs and which the plan's disk math records.
Goals.R-7: Guides and FAQ (mark-site repository): guide/faq.md gains an entry phrased as a question like every other entry in that file — "Mark will not start after an update — how do I roll back?" — with the exact commands per OS (the binary invoked by full path, e.g. /Applications/Mark.app/Contents/MacOS/mark --rollback on macOS and the installed executable path with --rollback on Windows, pinned against the real installer layouts at plan time), the --yes non-interactive form, the exit-code table (including that code 2 is clap usage errors), the first-hop limitation stated in plain words (the rollback safety net starts with the first update performed by a version that already contains it), the hint to adjust the path when Mark is not installed in the default location, and the quit-Mark-first advice for the case where a live but broken instance cannot show the confirmation dialog, and the release-history manual-download fallback for the cases the CLI reports as exits 4 and 7 (missing Windows asset, pre-rotation signature); guide/cli.md adds --rollback (and --yes) to its flags documentation. mark-site carries no GRACE governance, so this is a plain reviewed PR in that repository, executed in the same wave as the code, not a bundle of this change.
Goals.R-8: Governance: a new governed Rust module (the next free M-0NN id; the plan confirms availability before claiming) owns the rollback manager (prepare, digest, validate, restore, manifest lifecycle), with a matching V-M-0NN verification anchor routing its commands, scenarios and content-free markers in the same bundle as the code. Touched existing files (m020_cli.rs, main.rs boot order and single-instance-adjacent routing, m009_menu.rs, the renderer update path in commands/index.js and autoUpdates.js surface state) get VERSION bumps and CHANGE_SUMMARY entries per the modification checklist. The ten-locale rule covers the dialog and any notices; the menu label follows the existing Rust menu-string convention (English, like the other app-specific m009 labels); headless CLI terminal output is English-only, matching the existing English-only Rust-side strings (e.g. the store-managed updater message).
Goals.R-9: Channel gating: every rollback surface (menu item, CLI behavior, manifest writes) is gated to desktop builds exactly like the updater itself — the app-store Cargo feature and the M-048 build-mode descriptor (buildCapabilities.updater) — so store builds show no update-adjacent surface, per the standing App Store rule already enforced for file.check-update.

Fail-closed ordering is binding: prepare (snapshot + digest) strictly precedes downloadAndInstall; validation and digest re-verification strictly precede any swap or installer spawn; on macOS the bundle swap strictly precedes the preferences restore, while on Windows the preferences and skip writes precede the installer spawn and the manifest is finalized only after confirmed success (the restored version clears it at next launch); a failed or mismatched verification never executes a downloaded installer and never swaps the running bundle.

The updater feed, endpoints, signature scheme and update statistics are untouched: this change adds no telemetry and no network calls beyond the two Windows restore fetches (the release's latest.json signature asset and the installer itself); macOS restore is fully offline; latest.json and the release pipeline are not modified.

Existing gates stay green and unweakened: npm test, cargo test, renderer suites, e2e; grace lint current shows no new errors beyond the recorded pre-existing baseline; the 30 MB shipped-bundle footprint budget is not affected (staged copies live in the data root).
Store-rule compliance: app-store builds expose no rollback surface anywhere (menu, CLI, settings), matching the existing file.check-update gating and the M-048 capability map.
No release or train admission follows from approval: version bumps, tags and publication stay behind the separate owner release workflow.

Two consecutive clean four-corner review passes (Correctness and Contracts; Security and Privacy; UX and Docs; Performance and Footprint) over this spec and its corner matrix are recorded in design-context.xml before owner approval is requested.

NonGoals.NonGoal: Multi-step rollback history, version vaults or side-by-side installs (JetBrains-style version lists): exactly one previous version, refreshed by each update.
Server-driven fleet rollback (responding to the feed with a lower version and a custom version_comparator): a separate future change if ever needed; this change is strictly user-initiated.
Automatic crash-loop detection and auto-rollback: heuristics and false-positive risk are out of scope for v1.
Rollback surfaces in app-store builds (MAS, TestFlight): store channels manage their own versions (TestFlight already exposes previous builds).

OS code-signing (Authenticode) for the Windows installer: the release pipeline signs updates with the updater's ed25519 key; changing the signing pipeline is out of scope — the restore reuses that existing anchor.
Update statistics, feed endpoints, staged rollouts or any telemetry: a separate future change; this change adds no counting or reporting.
Creating plan.xml in this pass; implementing any R-item; claiming the new module id in the live graph before the plan confirms availability.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Snapshot: a successful in-app update always leaves a valid rollback set (macOS: staged bundle copy + preferences snapshot + manifest with SHA-256 digests; Windows: manifest with the validated previous version); an update whose preparation fails never downloads or installs anything and reports why; a failed download or install after a successful prepare leaves the previous live set untouched (promotion happens only after success); an interrupted preparation leaves no half-valid manifest (atomic staging verified by test) and a stale temp sibling is removed at the next prepare or restore; app-store builds never write a rollback manifest at all.

Validity and integrity: manifest validity is strict (schema, semver version, platform match, staged paths under the data root, stored data consistent with the deterministic derivation, and a recorded previous version equal to the running version is rejected as the failed-attempt state); an invalid, corrupted or tampered manifest behaves exactly like a missing one (no menu item, CLI exit 7, nothing applied, no network access); before any swap the staged artifacts are re-verified against the recorded digests and a mismatch aborts with the current state untouched (exit 6).

Menu path: "Roll Back to Mark {version}…" appears in Help only when a valid manifest exists and only in desktop builds; confirmation names the version, the settings revert and the skip of the departed version; cancel is a no-op; the whole flow emits the structured markers listed in the verification anchor.

CLI path: --rollback restores headless with TTY y/N confirmation that prints the target version, the settings revert and the skip of the departed version; manifest validity is resolved before the live-instance probe (exit 7 wins over delegation); non-interactive runs require --yes and decline without it (exit 5); the exit codes 0/3/4/5/6/7 behave as specified (code 2 stays clap's usage-error exit; exit 0 covers a completed restore, a successful delegation and the Windows installer-spawned-pending case, distinguished by the machine-readable line) and are printed in a stable machine-readable form; with a healthy instance running, a second launch of mark --rollback delegates to the running app's confirmation dialog — no headless swap, no second process, a repeated invocation while the dialog is open focuses it instead of stacking another, and an instance that cannot show the dialog makes the command decline with exit 6 and quit-first instructions (never a swap under a live instance).

Windows restore: the previous installer is fetched by its deterministically derived release asset name (strict semver derivation from the manifest, nothing else may be fetched or executed — pinned by an injected-path-material test), its minisignature from that release's latest.json is verified against the app-pinned updater pubkey, the fetched feed's version field equals the manifest's previous version, the executed bytes are the verified bytes (re-digested or spawned from the verified handle immediately before execution), and the installer is executed only after all checks pass; mismatch or download failure leaves the rollback set intact and exits 4; an installer run that fails after verification keeps the set and is detected by the departed version at its next launch, which re-offers an idempotent retry (the CLI has already exited 0 with the outcome pending); releases published without the Windows asset are covered by the documented release-history fallback, not by silent failure.

Skip semantics: after any restore, skippedUpdateVersion equals the departed version and the existing exact-match skip logic (autoUpdates.js) suppresses only that version; a subsequently released newer version shows the notice again normally.

Preferences safety: restore writes the pre-update snapshot over the canonical preferences file atomically; if the preferences step fails after a bundle swap, the restore still completes, boots the old version, and logs the skipped step (old code tolerating unknown newer keys is re-verified by test at plan time).

Depth and footprint: exactly one rollback set exists at any time; a new update refreshes it and cleans the old staging; a successful restore deletes the entire staging directory; a repeated --rollback with no set behaves as the no-snapshot case (exit 7, actionable message); the data-root peak during staging is bounded at 2x bundle size by design (≈ 64 MB at v2.8.2 sizes), this change's additions do not grow the shipped macOS bundle beyond the recorded baseline (≈ 32 MB on disk at v2.8.2; the historical under-30 MB Phase-B on-disk target is a pre-existing miss this change does not worsen), and the CI-enforced 20 MB Windows installer gate keeps passing.

Docs: mark-site guide/faq.md contains a question-form crash-recovery entry with exact per-OS commands, the --yes form, the exit-code table (code 2 = clap usage errors; Windows exit 0 = installer spawned, outcome pending), the first-hop limitation in plain words, the adjust-the-path hint for non-default install locations, the quit-Mark-first advice for a broken live instance, and the release-history manual-download fallback for exits 4 and 7; guide/cli.md documents --rollback and --yes; command paths match the real installer layouts (verified at plan time); the site check-dist gate stays green.

Assumptions.Assumption: Repository facts verified while drafting (2026-10-28): the updater feed is a single forward-only latest.json on GitHub Releases (tauri.conf.json:80-82); installSignedUpdate at commands/index.js:1195-1217 is the only download/install call site and always follows an explicit user click; nothing preserves the old bundle after an update; skippedUpdateVersion exists with exact-match semantics (autoUpdates.js:58, 229-241) and is persisted through the app-level preferences file (renderer ipc prefs facade), so the headless path can write it; m005_prefs refuses nothing on downgrade — the schema_version comparison only stamps (m005_prefs.rs:173-184) and writes are atomic (:113-134); argv is parsed by clap in m020_cli.rs before boot (main.rs:263), and clap itself exits with code 2 on usage errors (m020_cli.rs uses CliArgs::parse), which this change therefore never reassigns; the single-instance plugin registers during app init (main.rs:371-435), after all pre-boot main() code — hence the pre-boot probe in R-5; the CLI is not installed into any shell bin directory (mark-site guide/cli.md says so); GitHub Releases keeps all historical assets, with the Windows artifact set (setup.exe and its feed signature inside latest.json) present only on releases published with the WINDOWS_RELEASE repo variable enabled (release.yml stages it behind that variable); desktop bundle footprint: the installed .app measures ≈ 32 MB on disk at v2.8.2 (measured from the release tarball; the compressed downloads are ≈ 14 MB; the historical Phase-B on-disk target of under 30 MB predates this measurement and today's CI bundle-size step warns rather than fails), so the staged-copy cost is ≈ 32 MB steady-state with a ≈ 64 MB transient peak, and the plan's disk math uses the actual on-disk bundle size.

The rollback feature becomes effective for updates performed by versions that already contain it: a user updating from a pre-feature version to the first feature-carrying release has no rollback set for that hop (the old version's code could not snapshot itself); the FAQ entry states this honestly. From the next update on, every hop is covered.

macOS restore copies made by the running app itself carry no quarantine attribute and keep their original signature, so Gatekeeper does not intervene (Sparkle-style self-replacement precedent); on Windows the installer is not OS-code-signed today — authenticity of the restore download comes from the minisign check against the app-pinned updater pubkey (the same anchor as every update), and the NSIS passive install is the same installation mechanism the updater itself already triggers (installMode passive, tauri.conf.json:84-86). Both claims are re-verified during implementation.
